claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a naturally formed surface oxide while retaining its native microstructural features.
Controlled thermal oxidation or chemical removal followed by repassivation can create a uniform, dense, continuous oxide film on Q235 steel.
The proposed surface pretreatment can form the oxide film without altering the underlying Q235 microstructure.
A dense protective oxide film will delay corrosion onset relative to untreated Q235 steel.
A dense protective oxide film will reduce corrosion progression and corrosion rate relative to untreated Q235 steel.
The integrity, continuity, and chemical composition of the surface oxide film govern corrosion suppression.
A uniform, dense oxide film limits ingress of oxygen, moisture, and corrosive species to the steel substrate.
Limiting ingress through the oxide film reduces active sites for corrosion initiation.
An untreated or discontinuous oxide film permits faster penetration of aggressive species and accelerates corrosion.
Pretreated Q235 samples will show fewer pits and less flaking than untreated samples.
Untreated Q235 steel has a potentially uneven native oxide layer.
The proposed protective effect applies at room temperature and approximately 60°C under humid, chloride-containing exposure.
The protective effect may differ under temperatures or chemical conditions outside the proposed laboratory range.
The optimal protective oxide thickness, composition, and microstructural quality for Q235 steel are uncertain.
Microstructural features other than the oxide film may contribute to Q235 corrosion resistance and may not be isolated by the pretreatment.

Failure to obtain a statistically significant delay in corrosion onset and reduction in corrosion rate, or failure of the treated film to outlast the native oxide, is proposed as falsifying the oxide-mediated suppression hypothesis.
